description: Our team is filled with knowledge seeking innovators who are deeply committed to transforming informative web development. We are focused on creating an interactive site where users can track extrasolar objects and our skills in programming and web design are the catalyst for how we will complete our objective.
summary: For our objective of developing a public-facing web tool that utilizes images from SPHEREx to show change over time in space, we developed an interactive website that allows users to observe the behavior of different objects in the observable universe. We implement data sets from NASA’s SPHEREx telescope which records movement of objects by taking pictures over a given period of time using infrared. It's important because its an accessible experience for anyone of any age to witness movement of objects in space and explore their curiosity. It also expands upon the possibilities of mapping or predicting extrasolar activity.
details: Vantage turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations into an interactive way to explore how the sky changes over time. Users choose a prepared target or enter sky coordinates and a field of view, discover available observations, and play dated views of the same region. Frame comparison, pixel inspection, wavelength information, quality indicators, and shareable views help visitors connect what they see to the underlying measurements. Prepared examples include nearby stars, brown dwarfs, variable stars, and Ceres as a positional-motion example. The workflow starts with authentic SPHEREx FITS products from NASA/IPAC IRSA. A Python backend reads image, flag, variance, celestial-coordinate, and spectral-calibration information and aligns observations to a common sky grid. The browser presents the images with their actual acquisition dates and source provenance. Prepared examples use Quick Release 2 observations; live archive workflows use DR1 and Quick Release 3 products. Gaia DR3 and AllWISE provide optional catalog context, while JPL Horizons supplies predicted positions for Solar System examples. Catalog markers and predictions are distinguished from detections. We built the interface with React, TypeScript, CSS, and Vite, and used Python, Astropy, NumPy, and SciPy for astronomy data handling and processing. The frontend is hosted on Vercel. Live retrieval and processing currently depend on our computer-hosted backend and a temporary tunnel; prepared examples remain available independently. Our creative focus is making the time dimension of infrared astronomy approachable without hiding scientific limitations. Different wavelengths, missing coverage, image defects, foreground emission, and unequal observation intervals can create misleading comparisons, so Vantage makes those conditions visible. Visual changes are starting points for exploration, not automatic claims of motion, variability, or discovery. Quantitative comparisons require compatible wavelength coverage, registration, uncertainty checks, and appropriate point-spread-function treatment. The intended impact is to give students, educators, and curious members of the public a direct, traceable route from a sky location to real observations, helping them form questions about moving objects and changing sources. Use of Super Intelligence: We used Google NotebookLM during early research to build an introduction to relevant datasets and documentation, organize information about what those resources contain, and explore possible project modules such as temporal playback, coordinate search, image comparison, and catalog context. It helped structure our research and identify questions to verify against original sources. Displayed astronomical observations come from the cited archives; they are not SI-generated observations.
